Oh Anthropic Nvidia Corp.’s stock was up about 31% yesterday on news of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive officer. The Nasdaq 100 Index was up almost 7%, and in general the artificial intelligence trade came roaring back after a tough week last week. Anthropic PBC, though, was down 1.4% yesterday, closing at $87.64, just 5.6% above the $83 share price of its initial public offering last week. It fell again this morning, breaking below the IPO price ; at noon it was trading at about $77.39. It is early yet, but I wonder what Anthropic’s correlation with Jensen Huang is. On the one hand: Anthropic’s rise from nothing to a trillion-dollar valuation occurred at around the same time as Nvidia’s rise from about $320 billion to about $4 trillion yesterday. The same broad forces have been similarly good for Nvidia and Anthropic. There is a general broad artificial intelligence trade, in which investors bet on the speed and scale of the AI revolution, and Anthropic and Nvidia are big parts of it. When investors get enthusiastic about the AI trade, they buy Nvidia and Anthropic stock; when they get nervous, they sell. Nvidia and Anthropic are correlated in the minds and portfolios of investors. That AI trade depends heavily on raising trillions of dollars to finance AI infrastructure. Anthropic needs lots of that financing to pay for computing power, and Nvidia and Huang are crucial to that economy, as a provider of collateral and a coordinator of financing. That’s true in general — Nvidia is mobilizing hundreds of billions of dollars of chip financing, etc. — and also for Anthropic specifically: Anthropic has a “ strategic partnership with NVIDIA ,” and Nvidia was an anchor investor in Anthropic’s IPO. On the other hand, there is a basic rivalry between Nvidia and frontier AI labs like Anthropic. AI will, the market assumes, create trillions of dollars of value, and the battle is over who will capture that value. One is that you make a list of the stocks you want to buy, and you buy them. If you have a good reason to buy a stock, you buy it; if not, not. The default is not. If you have no opinions about a stock, you don’t buy it. The other is that you make a list of the stocks in the world, and for each stock on the list, you ask yourself: “Do I have a reason to overweight or underweight this stock?” The default is owning the market portfolio: If you have no opinions about a stock, or ambivalent or confused opinions, you tend to just own the average amount of the stock, its market capitalization weighting in the market portfolio. If you have reason to think that the stock is better than the market thinks it is, buy more of it. If you have reason to think that it’s worse than the market thinks it is, buy less of it, or zero, or go short. But you start from the premise that the market has a pretty good idea of what stocks to own, and that if you have no special information, then you should just do what the market tells you. I think it is fair to say that the second approach — defaulting to the market weight and overweighting or underweighting when you have reason to — was virtually unheard-of 100 years ago and is quite standard now. Many, many investors mostly buy index funds: They assume that the market knows better than they do, so they buy the stocks that the market likes. But many active investors use the same intellectual framework: They run large diversified portfolios and pick stocks to overweight and underweight against the background assumption that the default is the market weight. A company says it wants to raise $1 billion by selling 100 million shares at $10 each. Its bankers go out to investors, who put in orders for the shares. The bankers collect orders for, say, 700 million shares. “The IPO is seven times oversubscribed,” they say. [1] The IPO prices, and the bankers and company get together to “allocate” the IPO: There are orders for 700 million shares, but the company is selling only 100 million shares (actually 115 million with the greenshoe ), so most of the orders won’t get filled. The banks and company will favor some investors (long-term investors who understand the company’s story, the banks’ favorite clients, retail, whatever) and zero others (fast-money hedge funds that will flip the shares, etc.), but even the favored investors will probably get cut back. If you put in an order for 10 million shares, and the book is seven times covered, you’re not realistically going to get more than 5 million, and 2 million is more likely. But you know that, of course. If you have a sense that it will be a hot IPO — for instance because your salesperson at the bank says “this is a hot IPO and we’re getting a lot of demand” — you can scale up your order to try to get more shares. If you want 5 million shares, put in an order for 20 million. That way you’ll probably get cut back to 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 million. Sometimes you’ll mis-calibrate and end up with 1 million, or 10 million, either of which would be bad. (If you get 1 million, you’ll have to buy more when the stock starts trading, and if you got cut back to 1 million that probably means it will trade up. If you get 10 million, the reverse: You’ll have to sell when the stock starts trading, and if you got allocated so many shares, that’s a bad sign for demand.) But in a hot IPO, many investors are putting in orders for more shares than they want. [2] Or that is the stereotype. I have sometimes wondered if it applies to the new wave of mega-IPOs. What if Dario Amodei got caught having an affair with a spy, and another affair with his subordinate at Anthropic PBC? Well. The spy stuff could be bad for Anthropic: Anthropic’s products have serious national security consequences, and there might be regulatory repercussions; its business might be restricted to prevent its models from falling into the wrong hands. I don’t know about the subordinate stuff; I assume a lot of people working in AI live in polyamorous group houses with their coworkers so maybe that’s no big deal. What would happen to Amodei? I don’t know. But the flowchart is something like this: Anthropic’s board of directors would meet and decide what to do with him, weighing what various stakeholders — employees, suppliers, customers, governments, shareholders, etc. — want and their own sense of what would be best for the company and for the safe development of advanced artificial intelligence. Anthropic’s board has seven members, two of whom are Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, so that might be awkward. The board ultimately answers to a higher authority . Actually two higher authorities, or two and a half. Three of the seven board members are appointed by a “long-term benefit trust” made up of disinterested trustees whose job is to make sure that Anthropic builds AI safely for the benefit of humanity. Three are appointed by Anthropic’s seven co-founders. The seventh is appointed by the trust, but subject to the approval of the rest of the board, with Anthropic’s shareholders breaking any deadlocks. So the board would probably put more weight on the views of Anthropic’s co-founders and employees than would a normal public company board.
